newsitem.title: USA: New England suffers heavy damage in 'northeaster'.
newsitem.headline: New England suffers heavy damage in 'northeaster'.

text.p: As storm waters receded Tuesday, the New England region faced damages estimated in the tens of millions of dollars, emergency management officials said.

The fierce "northeaster," which poured more than a foot-and-a-half of rain in parts of the six-state region, has washed out roads and bridges, flooded homes and brought havoc to the area's transportation systems.
Peter LaPorte, head of the Massachusetts Emergency Management Agency, said in a telephone interview that the storm caused "tens of millions of dollars in damages" to the eastern part of the state.

New Hampshire Gov. Stephen Merrill said through a spokesman that more than 40 communities in eight of the state's 10 counties had reported severe damage to property and roads. "We have a rough preliminary estimate of $5.0 to $7.0 million in damages," said Merrill's spokesman, Jim Rivers.
In Maine, "we're estimating damages of at least $10 million," said a spokesman for Gov. Angus King.
The Maine Emergency Management Agency said it was still too early to assess the extent of the damages. Parts of Maine received more than 19 inches of rain (48.7 cm).
Rainwater broke the primary supply pipe of the Portland Water District, leaving 140,000 residents of the state's largest city and surrounding communities without drinking water Tuesday.
Travel remained difficult through the region. A 100-foot section of the Maine Turnpike was washed out.
In Boston, portions of the city's subway system remained closed because of flood damage on Monday at Kenmore Square. The important junction remained under water a day after the storm left the city.

Still, officials of the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, which operate Boston's subway system, were pleased with progress made by Tuesday afternoon. Pumps had been able lower the depth of water covering the tracks to six-and-a-half feet from 20-feet on Monday.
